title: The Song of Songs
lead: The Song of Songs is a book of Hebrew love poems with no mention of God's covenant and, apart from the debated 'flame of Yah' in 8:6, no divine name. Jews and Christians have read it for almost two thousand years as the love of God for Israel, or of Christ for the Church or the soul, and most modern scholars read it first as poetry about human love. Each reading has shaped worship, prayer and marriage.

sections.h: Love and marriage as a picture of God and his people
sections.b:
The Bible often speaks of God's covenant as a marriage. Hosea 2:14–20 pictures God courting Israel in the wilderness and betrothing her; Isaiah 54:5 and Isaiah 62:5 call God Israel's husband and Zion his bride; Jeremiah 2:2 remembers Israel's love as a bride; Ezekiel 16 tells the history of Jerusalem as a foundling girl who becomes God's wife and betrays him. These passages do not quote the Song, but they gave the Jewish and Christian readers of the Song the language they used to read it as a book about God.

In the New Testament Jesus calls himself the bridegroom (Mark 2:19–20), John the Baptist speaks of the groom's friend (John 3:29), Paul calls the Church the bride of Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2; Ephesians 5:25–32), and Revelation ends with the wedding of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9; Revelation 21:2). The Song is not quoted in any of these.

sections.h: Human love in the rest of Scripture
sections.b: The Song stands among other biblical praises of human love. Genesis 2:23–25 has the first poem of a man delighted by a woman. Proverbs 5:15–20 tells a husband to drink from his own cistern and to be taken captive by his wife's love, and Proverbs 7:6–23 shows the other side, the bed perfumed with myrrh, aloes and cinnamon in the house of the foreign woman. Ecclesiastes 9:9 tells the reader to enjoy life with the wife he loves. Psalm 45 is a royal wedding song with myrrh, aloes and cassia. Isaiah 5:1–7 begins as a love song about a vineyard.

sections.h: The book's place in the canon
sections.b: The Song was one of the books whose place in the canon was argued among the rabbis. The Mishnah records that Rabbi Akiva said the world was never as worthy as on the day the Song was given to Israel, since all the Writings are holy but the Song is the holy of holies (Mishnah Yadayim 3:5). Another rabbinic passage condemns anyone who sings it in a banquet house as if it were an ordinary song (Tosefta Sanhedrin 12:10). In the Christian church the Song's place was never seriously in doubt, though Theodore of Mopsuestia (about AD 400) is reported to have rejected the allegorical reading, and Sebastian Castellio, in Geneva in 1544, is said to have called it a lascivious poem. The Song's place among the five Scrolls read in the synagogue, with Passover for the Song, is a later custom.
